Occult historian Peter Levenda has written on the links between esoteric orders, intelligence agencies, and dark religion for decades. On Danny Jones's podcast, he brings that lens to three subjects: newly released Epstein files, the ancient god Baal, and the modern Church of Satan.

Levenda's method treats ritual and power as old partners, and he reads the Epstein record through that partnership. Jones follows him from ancient sacrifice to twentieth-century occult movements. The connections Levenda draws are his own scholarship and speculation mixed, and listeners should keep the seam in view. Few guests can move between archaeology and current scandal in one argument; whether the argument persuades, it is unlike anything else in this series.
podcast-dannyjones-NJp2rASRKMc:
Researcher Danny Goler ran an informal experiment in which volunteers used DMT under observation and reported their experiences. He joins Danny Jones to discuss its strangest result. Many subjects described the same symbols. Goler presents them as an alien code hidden in the fabric of reality.

The experiment leaned on laser light and repeated sessions, and Goler describes the shared imagery his subjects reported seeing. Jones presses him on suggestion, expectation, and what would falsify the code idea. The work sits far outside controlled science, and Goler's reading of it is his own. The episode preserves a claim currently spreading through psychedelic culture at the moment of its making, in its maker's voice. Listeners can judge whether the pattern sounds like discovery or like the oldest trap in the study of visions.
podcast-dannyjones-cowUWvuukmc:
Author Gregg Braden joins Danny Jones for a talk that links God, new tech, aliens, and the start of human life. The episode title bills him as a biblical geologist. Braden is known for mixing science and faith in his books.

Braden lays out his view that old texts and new finds point the same way. He talks about human roots, lost skill, and signs of design in nature. Jones asks where his claims rest on digs and where they rest on faith. Listeners get Braden's full case in one long sitting. The library holds the talk as an archive record.
